title: When rehat is broken
hook: breaking the code is met with a penance set by five Sikhs

segments.voice: Yesterday, the instructions after amrit: a new family, the banis, the five Ks, the things to avoid. Your line was what is promised. What did you say back, plainly, so both of you heard it? Day one thousand two hundred seventy-four.

This week has been full of words said out loud: four rounds at a wedding, a prayer at the pyre, five Sikhs giving amrit, the rehat explained before anyone leaves. Which leaves the question nobody likes to ask at a ceremony. What happens when someone breaks it? Not in a dramatic way. A person who promised, and meant it, slips. A rule bends, then gives. In some everyday groups, an office, a team, a family, that gets handled with silence: nobody mentions it, and the person drifts to the back row, then out the door. The Sikh code takes a different road. It walks the person to the front. Today's word is tankhah.
screen: `A WEEK OF WORDS SAID ALOUD.` → `WHAT IF ONE IS BROKEN?` → `THE CODE WALKS YOU TO THE FRONT.`

segments.voice: Tankhah is the penance set for a Sikh who has broken the code. Someone under tankhah is called a tankhaiya. Here is the process in the Sikh Rehat Maryada, paraphrased. The person goes to the nearest sangat, the gathered congregation, and stands before it, in the presence of the Guru Granth Sahib. There they say what they did. No one has to drag it out of them; the code expects the person to come. Then five Sikhs, chosen from the sangat and in good standing under the code, hear the case. They decide the tankhah. The person accepts it without arguing back. And the matter closes with an ardas, the standing prayer, offered for them. Look at what that does. First, the confession is open. The mistake is not whispered to one person behind a curtain; it's owned in front of the community the promise was made to. Second, the judgment is shared. Not one elder with a grudge or a soft spot, but five, the same number that gives amrit. A person is welcomed in by five, and set right by five. Third, there is an end. The tankhah is set, carried out, and prayed over, and the person stands again as one of the sangat. The code doesn't leave a mark on them for life. For the gravest breaches, the four the instructions named yesterday, the code asks for something more: after penance, the person takes amrit again. For other lapses, the tankhah itself is the road back. What the process never offers is hiding. The way home goes through the front of the room. Own it.
screen: `TANKHAH: THE PENANCE FOR A BREACH.` · `CONFESSED BEFORE THE SANGAT.` · `FIVE SIKHS SET THE PENANCE.` · `AN ARDAS, AND IT IS CLOSED.` · then, large: `OWN IT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: own one mistake. Settle, and breathe. Let one recent mistake come to mind. Pick a small one; a two-minute sit is not the place for the biggest. Now say it to yourself in one plain sentence, starting with I. Not they made me, not it happened. I did this. Then add one more sentence: what would set it right. You don't have to do anything yet. Just let both sentences sit there, side by side, until the bell. The bell holds the time.
Tankhah. The penance set for a Sikh who has broken the code, decided by five Sikhs before the sangat and closed with an ardas. Today's word.

Your line: own it. Today, tell the person affected by one small mistake of yours, in one plain sentence, and ask what would make it right. That closes a week of promises. Day one thousand two hundred seventy-four.

trapdoor: what you thought: breaking a religious rule means punishment, or quietly drifting away.
what it means: tankhah is a penance set by five Sikhs after an open confession before the sangat.
what a scholar hears: the code ends it with an ardas, so the process aims at restoring the person to the sangat, not marking them.
